title: Psalm 139: Searched and Known
summary: David marvels that the LORD knows him completely, his sitting and rising, his thoughts and words before he speaks. There is nowhere he could go to escape God's presence, not the heavens, not Sheol, not the far sea or the darkness. God formed him in the womb and wrote his days in a book before any of them came to be. After asking God to slay the wicked who oppose him, David ends by asking God to search his own heart and lead him in the everlasting way.
story: Psalm 139 stands near the end of the Psalter in the final collection attributed to David (Psalms 138 to 145). After the thanksgiving of Psalm 138, which ended by asking God not to abandon the work of his hands, Psalm 139 reflects at length on what it means to be the work of God's hands, known from the womb onward. It is followed by a series of urgent prayers for protection from violent and deceitful enemies (Psalms 140 to 143). Psalm 139 prepares for them by establishing the ground of the psalmist's confidence: a God who knows everything, is present everywhere, and made him with care. Its closing request, “Search me, O God”, reverses the opening statement that the LORD has searched him, turning a fact into a prayer.
historical:
The heading reads “For the choirmaster. A Psalm of David.” The first phrase probably marks the psalm for use by the director of the temple music. As with other superscriptions, scholars debate whether “of David” names the author or records a later attribution. Traditional readers take it at face value. Many modern scholars date the psalm after the exile, partly because its Hebrew includes several words and forms that resemble Aramaic, the international language of the Persian period. Others answer that Aramaic influence on Hebrew is found in earlier texts too, and that poetic vocabulary is a weak guide to date.

Some scholars have suggested a specific setting: a person falsely accused, perhaps of idolatry, appealing to God for vindication at the sanctuary. On this reading, the psalm's opening affirms that God already knows the truth about the accused, verses 19 to 22 distance him from God's enemies, and verses 23 and 24 invite God to test his innocence. Old Testament law provided for cases decided before God at the sanctuary (1 Kings 8:31-32). This reading is possible but not certain, and the psalm's language is general enough to be prayed in many situations.
cultural:
Sheol, in verse 8, was the Old Testament name for the realm of the dead, pictured as a shadowy place below the earth where all the dead went. Many psalms describe it as a place cut off from God's praise (Psalm 6:5 and 88:10-12). Psalm 139 makes a startling claim: even there, God is present. The wings of the dawn (verse 9) picture the far east where the sun rises, and the farthest sea is the Mediterranean to the west; together they span the whole known world.

The images of forming in the womb draw on ancient crafts. God knit the psalmist together (verse 13), and he was woven together in the depths of the earth (verse 15), language used for embroidery or intricate weaving. The phrase “the depths of the earth” is probably a poetic image for the hidden, dark place of the womb, and perhaps also recalls humanity's origin from the dust (Genesis 2:7). The inmost being in verse 13 is literally the kidneys, which the Hebrews regarded as the seat of the deepest emotions and moral life. A book in which days are written (verse 16) reflects the ancient practice of royal records and registers, and Scripture elsewhere speaks of God's book of the living (Psalm 69:28 and Exodus 32:32).
literary: Psalm 139 is often classed as a wisdom or meditative psalm, though it ends with elements of lament and a plea for vindication. It moves in four stanzas of roughly six verses each. Verses 1 to 6 celebrate God's knowledge: the verb know appears repeatedly, and the stanza ends in wonder. Verses 7 to 12 celebrate God's presence, using a series of if clauses (heaven, Sheol, dawn, sea, darkness) that each end with God already there. Verses 13 to 18 celebrate God's creative work in the womb and the vastness of his thoughts. Verses 19 to 24 turn abruptly to the wicked and then back to the psalmist's own heart. The psalm is framed by its first and last lines: “You have searched me and known me” in verse 1 and “Search me, O God, and know my heart” in verse 23.

outline.t: Formed in the womb, written in God's book

doctrines.note: The psalm is Scripture's fullest poetic description of what theologians call God's omniscience (he knows everything) and omnipresence (he is present everywhere). It presents these not as abstract ideas but as the reality of being personally known and personally accompanied.

Every human life is formed by God from its hidden beginnings. The psalmist's wonder at being fearfully and wonderfully made grounds the dignity of the body and of human life before birth, which the church has long drawn on in affirming the value of the unborn.

All the psalmist's days were written in God's book before one of them came to be. Readers differ over how detailed a plan this implies, but the psalm presents it as comfort, not fatalism: no part of life lies outside God's care.

words.note: Yada, to know. The verb appears six times in the psalm. In Hebrew, knowing is often relational and experiential rather than merely factual; it can describe the knowledge of a friend or a spouse. God's knowledge of the psalmist is complete and personal. The psalm ends with the psalmist asking to be known even more deeply.

Sheol, the grave or the realm of the dead. For many psalmists Sheol was the place farthest from God, where no one praised him. Verse 8 insists that God is there too. The claim does not yet amount to a full doctrine of resurrection, but it points toward the hope that death cannot separate God's people from him.

Golem, unformed body or embryo. The word occurs only here in the Old Testament and refers to something rolled up or unshaped. It describes the psalmist before his body was fully formed, and it says that God saw him even then. It is a key word in Christian reflection on the value of unborn life.

Chaqar, to search or examine. The verb describes careful investigation, like searching out a land or examining a case. It opens the psalm (the LORD has searched me) and returns in the final prayer (search me). The psalmist moves from being searched to asking to be searched, welcoming God's scrutiny.

christ: The New Testament presents Jesus as the one who knows what is in every person. John notes that Jesus did not need anyone to testify about man, for he knew what was in a man (John 2:25), and Hebrews says no creature is hidden from God's sight (Hebrews 4:13). The psalm's confidence that God's presence reaches even into Sheol finds its fullest answer in Christ, who entered death itself and rose, so that Paul can say that neither death nor life nor height nor depth can separate us from the love of God in Christ Jesus our Lord (Romans 8:38-39). The psalm's wonder at the forming of a human life in the womb also takes on new weight in the incarnation: the eternal Son was himself knit together in a mother's womb. These connections are thematic, not predictive, but they show the psalm's God fully revealed.

hard.q: How can a psalm about God's intimate care end with “I hate them with perfect hatred”?
hard.a: The turn in verses 19 to 22 surprises many readers. After meditating on God's tender care, the psalmist asks God to slay the wicked and declares that he hates those who hate God. Several considerations help. The enemies here are described as bloodthirsty men who speak of God deceitfully and take his name in vain; the psalmist identifies with God's cause against those who oppose him, not against personal rivals. The perfect hatred of verse 22 means a complete refusal to side with evil, a total rejection of the enemies' cause, and in Hebrew idiom hate can mean to reject or to refuse allegiance, not only to feel emotional loathing. Most striking, the psalmist immediately turns the searchlight on himself: “Search me, O God, and know my heart.” He does not exempt himself from God's scrutiny. Christians read these verses in light of Jesus' command to love enemies (Matthew 5:44). Some see the psalm's hatred as rejection of evil itself, which Christians must share; others see here a sentiment that the gospel transforms. Either way, the psalm models a person who opposes evil while inviting God to root it out of his own heart first.

questions: Is the idea of being completely known by God more comforting or more unsettling to you? Why?
The psalmist says there is nowhere, not even darkness or death, where God is absent. Where have you felt farthest from God, and how does this psalm speak to that place?
The psalm ends by asking God to search the psalmist's own heart. What would it take for you to pray that prayer honestly?
